parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how the Earth itself spins and what the satellite must do to stay fixed above the same spot on the ground.
parts.proper_answer: west to east, same sense as the rotation of the Earth.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Staying fixed means moving with the Earth**
A geostationary satellite appears stationary above one point on the Equator. That can only happen if you travel round in the same sense as the surface below you. The Earth spins from west to east, so you must orbit from west to east too.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about where a satellite must be so that its circular orbit keeps it over the same latitude as the Earth turns underneath.
parts.proper_answer: directly above the Equator, in the equatorial plane.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Only one latitude works**
To remain over the same point, the centre of the orbit must be the centre of the Earth and the orbit must not drift north or south. That means the orbit lies in the plane of the Equator, with the satellite positioned above the Equator.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which part of the electromagnetic spectrum passes easily through the atmosphere and is used for satellite TV and phone links.
parts.proper_answer: e.g. $4 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}$ (any value in range $1 \times 10^9$ to $300 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Microwaves for space links**
Satellite to Earth communication uses microwaves, typically in the GHz region. They pass through the atmosphere with little absorption and can be focused into narrow beams by dishes. Any frequency of order a few GHz, for example $6 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}$, is acceptable.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking how a loss expressed in dB links the ratio of received power to transmitted power using a logarithm.
Hint 2: Remember to convert the starting power to watts and to use a negative sign for attenuation, then set up the logarithmic equation.
Hint 3: Rearrange to isolate the received power by dividing by 10 and then using the inverse log (10 to the power of).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the decibel rule for power**
For power, gain compares output to input on a log scale:
$$ \text{gain/dB} = 10 \lg \left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right) $$
Here $P_1$ is the transmitted power and $P_2$ is the received power. Attenuation means gain is negative.

Step 2: **Put in the numbers**
Convert $3.0 \text{ kW} = 3000 \text{ W}$ and use $-195 \text{ dB}$:
$$ -195 = 10 \lg \left(\frac{P}{3000}\right) $$
$$ \lg \left(\frac{P}{3000}\right) = -19.5 $$

Step 3: **Undo the log to find P**
$$ \frac{P}{3000} = 10^{-19.5} $$
$$ P = 3000 \times 10^{-19.5} \approx 9.5 \times 10^{-17} \text{ W} $$
This tiny value shows how greatly the signal is attenuated over the huge distance to the satellite.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Compare the size of your answer in (b)(i) with the kilowatt power sent out - think about how weak the up-link is when it arrives versus how strong the amplified down-link is when it leaves.
Hint 2: Think what would happen at the satellite receiver if the powerful outgoing signal and the tiny incoming signal were on the same frequency.
parts.proper_answer: The up-link signal is greatly attenuated to ~$10^{-16} \text{ W}$ on arrival, while the down-link is greatly amplified before re-transmission. Using different frequencies prevents the powerful down-link swamping the weak up-link signal.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Huge difference in power levels**
You found the up-link arrives with only about $10^{-16} \text{ W}$, after starting at $3000 \text{ W}$. At the satellite this very weak incoming signal sits right next to the transmitter sending a strong amplified signal back down to Earth.

Step 2: **Separate frequencies to avoid swamping**
If both used the same frequency, the powerful down-link transmission would overwhelm or interfere with the sensitive receiver trying to detect the tiny up-link. Using different carrier frequencies keeps them distinct, so the down-link does not swamp the up-link.
